Candidate-independent fusion uses fixed itemwise transforms: for example, s(u,i)=z(u,i)/T+α log(max(p(i|h),ε))+β log1p(q(u,i)/τ), with constants frozen after validation. This is a practical synthesis, not a single established algorithm. Avoid candidate-set min–max normalization, z-scores, or separately normalized probability mixtures: changing candidates changes component scales. Positive temperature scaling preserves neural ranking alone but changes its influence in fusion; classification calibration evidence does not establish full-catalog recommendation calibration. [Guo et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html)

Shrink sparse transitions toward a training-derived prior: p(i|j)=(c(j,i)+λp₀(i))/(n(j)+λ); low-support rows receive stronger relative shrinkage. Neighborhood alternatives include support-shrunk cosine and sparse learned weights. [SLIM](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220765374_SLIM_Sparse_Linear_Methods_for_Top-N_Recommender_Systems) learns sparse item–item coefficients and scores through history–weight multiplication. Practical inference: store top neighbors in CSR, accumulate contributions from recent history, score neural embeddings in catalog chunks, and maintain global top-k. Neighborhood truncation approximates the original model; retrieval-only reranking can miss fused winners. Smoothed transition priors also contribute outside stored edges and must remain represented.

With one positive and 99 negatives, sampled HR@10 measures top-ten placement among 100 candidates, not among all unseen items. Sampling can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; fixed itemwise scores ensure reproducibility across candidate regimes but cannot make their metrics equivalent. [Rendle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.02263) Therefore tune the required macro sampled validation HR@10, preserve identical scoring in full-catalog inference, and never interpret sampled improvements as demonstrated full-catalog gains.
